newsitem.title: CANADA: Chretien says more than majority needed on Quebec.
newsitem.headline: Chretien says more than majority needed on Quebec.

text.p: Prime Minister Jean Chretien said on Tuesday he would not let Canada split on the basis of a simple majority vote of Quebeckers seeking independence.

"The future of a nation and the protection of minorities -- do you let it go with one vote? I don't think so," Chretien said on Canadian Broadcasting Corp. (CBC). Separatists came within one percentage point of winning a referendum on Quebec sovereignty in October 1995.

Chretien said at that time he would not allow Canada to split on the basis of 50 percent plus one vote, but he was criticised by both the separatist Bloc Quebecois and the western Reform Party, which wanted the ground rules clear.

Speaking in a televised "town hall" format, answering questions from Canadians whom the CBC flew in to Ottawa, he made it clear he would insist on more than 50 percent. "I'm a democrat, but not by one vote," said the French-speaking Quebec native, who has fought to keep Canada united.

Chretien would not specify how much more than 50 percent would be enough in a new sovereignty referendum. But he noted: "Even to break up a factory in Quebec or a corporation you need two-thirds of the vote."

He also repeated that he would insist that any future referendum question clearly ask whether Quebec wished to leave Canada. He said last year's question, referring to Quebec making an offer of partnership with Canada, was fuzzy.
The sovereignty drive has lost momentum in Canada and support for it has slipped slightly in the polls, but analysts say an inspiring leader could reinvigorate it.

The separatist former premier of Quebec, Jacques Parizeau, one of the leaders of last year's campaign, is being urged by some colleagues to run for the leadership of the Bloc Quebecois in the federal Parliament.

Parizeau's partner in the referendum campaign, Lucien Bouchard, left the Bloc early this year to replace Parizeau as the head of Quebec's government. But some separatists now view Bouchard as too soft.

On economic issues, Chretien faced a combative audience, with several questions on when he would act to bring Canada's unemployment below 10 percent. He responded that Canada's job creation has been strong and while he was disappointed with the unemployment figures, "the government can't take everybody on the payroll."
